processing: Typical of Fenghuang Dancong: sun-withered, shaken and rested to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and dried or lightly roasted.
harvest_season: As with most Fenghuang Dancong, spring is the main picking.
appearance_dry: Typically long, straight, dark brown strips, as with other Dancong.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear orange-yellow, as with other Dancong.
appearance_wet: Typically long leaves, green with reddened edges, as with other Dancong.
taste_profile: Little is documented on the cup. The name points to fuzi, a medicinal root, but what that means in the aroma has not been described in any detail.

brewing.notes: As with other Dancong, keep the leaf load modest and pour off quickly.

vintage_note: Rarely listed. As is usual for Dancong, it would be sold by spring harvest of the current year, often with some months of rest after roasting.
description:
Fuzi Xiang is one of the lesser-known names in the Fenghuang Dancong family. Chinese lists of aroma types place it outside the ten standard ones, among strains such as pomelo blossom and orange blossom.

Fuzi is a word used for a root in Chinese medicine, which suggests a warm, medicinal note rather than a flower, though that is a reading of the name and not a documented tasting note.

It would be made in the usual Dancong way, with sun withering, shaking, firing and rolling, and it should be brewed like other Dancong, with very short steeps.

If you find it, ask whether the name refers to a particular strain, and treat it as an experiment rather than a known quantity.
history: Little is documented beyond its appearance in lists of Fenghuang aroma types and strains. Who selected it, and when, is not recorded in anything readily available.
